summary: Describes a mechanism for signaling that compression is wanted for SIP messages, and states when it is appropriate to send compressed SIP messages to another SIP entity. It builds on the Signaling Compression framework.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP messages can be compressed to make them smaller, but the two ends have to agree first. This RFC gives SIP a way to say so: a parameter called comp=sigcomp on the address or on the Via header. An endpoint that sees it knows the other end will accept a compressed message, and it also knows the other end is willing to receive one.

questions: why not use dns to signal sip compression
subtitle: How SIP endpoints signal, with a simple URI and Via parameter, that they accept SigComp-compressed messages.

tldr.problem: SIP could advertise optional layers such as TLS or compression through DNS, but every combination of transport, security and compression would need its own DNS entry. A server with two transports, TLS and SigComp would need 8.
tldr.mechanism: A comp=sigcomp parameter on a SIP URI or on a Via header says the entity supports SigComp and is willing to receive compressed messages. Clients and servers then compress requests and responses only when they have seen it.
tldr.outcome: Compression is negotiated at the SIP layer with no extra DNS records. A compressed request to a server that does not understand SigComp cannot be answered, so clients retry uncompressed after a timeout. RFC 5049 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Token length
facts.value: SHOULD be no more than ten characters

today: RFC 3486 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2003. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5049, so read the two together.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A SIP client sending a request to a SIP server typically performs a DNS lookup for the domain name of the server. When NAPTR or SRV records are available for the server, the client can specify the type of service it wants. The service in this context is the transport protocol to be used by SIP, such as UDP, TCP or SCTP. A SIP server that supports three different transport protocols will have three different DNS entries.

Since the number of transport protocols supported by a particular application layer protocol is not going to grow dramatically, having a DNS entry per transport seems scalable enough. However, sometimes it is necessary to include new layers between the transport protocol and the application layer protocol, such as transport layer security and compression. If DNS were used to discover the availability of these layers for a particular server, the number of DNS entries needed for that server would grow dramatically.

A server that supported TCP and SCTP as transports, TLS for transport security and SigComp for signalling compression would need eight DNS entries: TCP with no security and no compression, TCP with no security and SigComp, TCP with TLS and no compression, TCP with TLS and SigComp, and the same four again for SCTP. It is clear that this way of using DNS is not scalable, so an application layer mechanism to express support of signalling compression is needed.

The document also notes that a SIP element that supports compression will need to be prepared to receive compressed and uncompressed messages on the same port. It will perform demultiplexing based on the cookie in the topmost bits of every compressed message.
sections.plainLanguage: Today a SIP server advertises what it can do through DNS, and one DNS entry covers one transport. Add TLS, add compression, and the number of entries multiplies: two transports, with and without security, with and without compression, is eight entries. This RFC avoids that by putting the compression signal in the SIP messages themselves.

sections.title: Overview of Operation
sections.content:
There are two types of SIP messages, SIP requests and SIP responses. Clients send SIP requests to the host part of a URI, and servers send responses to the host in the sent-by parameter of the Via header field.

The document defines two parameters, one for SIP URIs and the other for the Via header field. The format of both is the same, as shown in the examples:

sip:alice@atlanta.com;comp=sigcomp
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP server1.foo.com:5060;branch=z9hG4bK87a7;comp=sigcomp

The presence of this parameter in a URI indicates that the request has to be compressed using SigComp. Its presence in a Via header field indicates that the response has to be compressed using SigComp.

Therefore, the presence of comp=sigcomp indicates that the SIP entity identified by the URI or by the Via header field supports SigComp and is willing to receive compressed messages. Having comp=sigcomp mean willingness as well as support allows the receiver of a SIP message to influence the decision of whether or not to use SigComp at a given time.
sections.plainLanguage: One parameter, comp=sigcomp, says that the other end understands compressed messages and is willing to receive them. It can sit on the URI in a request or on the Via header field, where it means the same thing for responses.

sections.title: Sending a Request to a Server
sections.content:
A request is sent to the host part of a URI, called the next-hop URI, which is the Request-URI of the request or an entry in the Route header field. If the next-hop URI contains the parameter comp=sigcomp, the client SHOULD compress the request using SigComp. If the next-hop URI is a SIPS URI, the request SHOULD be compressed before it is passed to the TLS layer. A client MUST NOT send a compressed request to a server if it does not know whether or not the server supports SigComp.

Regardless of whether the request is sent compressed or not, if a client would like to receive subsequent requests within the same dialog in the UAS to UAC direction compressed, this client SHOULD add the parameter comp=sigcomp to the URI in the Contact header field if it is a user agent client. If the client is a proxy, it SHOULD add the parameter comp=sigcomp to its URI in the Record-Route header field. If a user agent client sends a compressed request, it SHOULD add the parameter comp=sigcomp to the URI in the Contact header field. If a proxy that Record-Routes sends a compressed request, it SHOULD add comp=sigcomp to its URI in the Record-Route header field. If a client sends a compressed request, it SHOULD add the parameter comp=sigcomp to the topmost entry of the Via header field.

If a client does not know whether or not the server supports SigComp, but in case the server supported it would like to receive compressed responses, the client SHOULD add the parameter comp=sigcomp to the topmost entry of the Via header field. The request itself will not be compressed.

For requests within a dialog, a next-hop URI with the comp=sigcomp parameter is obtained from a Record-Route header field when the dialog is established. A client sending a request outside a dialog can also obtain SIP URIs with comp=sigcomp in a Contact header field in a 3xx or 485 response to the request.

However, clients establishing a session will not typically be willing to wait until the dialog is established in order to begin compressing messages. One of the biggest gains SigComp can bring to SIP is the ability to compress the initial INVITE of a dialog, when the user is waiting for the session to be established, so clients need a means to obtain a comp=sigcomp URI from their outbound proxy before the user decides to establish a session.

One solution to this problem is manual configuration. Sometimes, however, clients have to be configured in an automatic fashion, and current mechanisms for SIP client configuration, such as using DHCP, do not allow URI parameters to be provided. In this case, the client SHOULD send an uncompressed OPTIONS request to its outbound proxy. The outbound proxy can provide an alternative SIP URI with the comp=sigcomp parameter in a Contact header field in a 200 OK response to the OPTIONS. The client can use this URI for subsequent requests that are sent through the same outbound proxy using compression.

RFC 3261 does not define how a proxy should respond to an OPTIONS request addressed to itself; it only describes how servers respond to OPTIONS addressed to a particular user. This document extends that behaviour to proxy servers responding to OPTIONS addressed to them. They MAY list a set of alternative URIs to contact the proxy. Receiving incoming requests, even initial INVITEs, compressed is not a problem, since user agents can REGISTER a SIP URI with comp=sigcomp in their registrar, and all incoming requests for the user will then be sent to this SIP URI using compression.
sections.plainLanguage: A client compresses a request only when the address it is sending to carries the comp=sigcomp parameter, and it must not send a compressed request at all if it does not know the server understands SigComp. To learn the parameter early, the client can send an uncompressed OPTIONS request to its outbound proxy, which answers with an alternative address that already has the parameter.

sections.title: Sending a Response to a Client
sections.content:
A response is sent to the host in the sent-by parameter of the Via header field. If the topmost Via header field contains the parameter comp=sigcomp, the response SHOULD be compressed. Otherwise, the response MUST NOT be compressed.

In order to avoid asymmetric compression, that is, two SIP entities exchanging compressed requests in one direction and uncompressed requests in the other direction, proxies need to rewrite their Record-Route entries in the responses. A proxy performing Record-Route inspects the Record-Route header field in the response and the Contact header field in the request that triggered this response. It looks for the URI of the next upstream, closer to the user agent client, hop in the route set. If this URI contains the parameter comp=sigcomp, the proxy SHOULD add comp=sigcomp to its entry in the Record-Route header field. If this URI does not contain the parameter comp=sigcomp, the proxy SHOULD remove comp=sigcomp, if it is present, from its entry in the Record-Route header field. The same way, a user agent server SHOULD add comp=sigcomp to the Contact header field of the response if the URI of the next upstream hop in the route set contained the parameter comp=sigcomp.

The document also covers double Record-Routing, where some proxies add two Record-Route entries to avoid Record-Route rewriting. A typical example is a SIP proxy that acts as a firewall between two networks: depending on which network a request comes from, it is received on a different interface by the proxy, and the proxy adds one Record-Route entry for one interface and a second one for the other. Proxies that receive compressed messages from one side of the dialog and uncompressed messages from the other MAY use the mechanism described above. If a proxy detects that the next-hop proxy for a request is the proxy itself and that the request will not be sent through the network, the proxy MAY choose not to compress the request even if the URI contains the comp=sigcomp parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: A response is compressed only when the topmost Via header field says comp=sigcomp. To keep both directions of a call in step, proxies rewrite their Record-Route entries in the response to match what the other end asked for.

sections.title: Error Situations
sections.content:
If a compressed SIP request arrives at a SIP server that does not understand SigComp, the server will not have any means to indicate the error to the client. The message will be impossible to parse, and there will be no Via header field indicating an address to send an error response.

If a SIP client sends a compressed request and the client transaction times out without having received any response, the client SHOULD retry the same request without using compression. If the compressed request was sent over a TCP connection, the client SHOULD close that connection and open a new one to send the uncompressed request. Otherwise the server would not be able to detect the beginning of the new message.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that cannot decompress a message cannot even report the error, so the client gets nothing back. The client therefore retries the request without compression, on a fresh TCP connection if it was using one.

sections.title: Augmented BNF and the Registry
sections.content:
The document gives the augmented Backus-Naur Form of both parameters. The compression URI parameter is a uri-parameter, as defined by the SIP ABNF:

compression-param  =  "comp=" ("sigcomp" / other-compression)
other-compression  =  token

via-compression    =  "comp" EQUAL ("sigcomp" / other-compression)
other-compression  =  token

The IANA Considerations section defines the comp URI parameter and the comp Via extension. New values for comp are registered by IANA when new signalling compression schemes are published in standards track RFCs. The IANA Considerations section of such an RFC must name the compression scheme and the token value to be used, and the token may be of any length but SHOULD be no more than ten characters long. At the time of writing, the only entry in the registry is Signaling Compression, token sigcomp, reference RFC 3486.
sections.plainLanguage: The two parameters have a simple shape: the word comp, an equals sign, and a token naming the compression scheme. Today the only registered scheme is sigcomp.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The example shows an INVITE, 200 OK and ACK exchange between a user agent client and a user agent server through two proxies. Proxy P1 does not Record-Route but proxy P2 does. Both proxies support compression, but they do not use it by default. The client is configured to send compressed traffic to P1, so it compresses the INVITE and adds the comp=sigcomp parameter to the Via and Contact header fields. P1 forwards the INVITE uncompressed. P2 forwards it uncompressed as well, and Record-Routes itself so that it stays in the signalling path.

When the 200 OK comes back, P2 looks at the route set. The next hop towards the client is the Contact header field of the INVITE, which carried comp=sigcomp, so P2 adds comp=sigcomp to its own Record-Route entry in the response. That lets the client send compressed requests within the dialog. P1 sends the 200 OK compressed to the client, because the Via header field contained the parameter. The client then sends the ACK compressed directly to P2, and P2 forwards it uncompressed to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example shows a call set up through two proxies. The client compresses what it sends to its own proxy, the proxies pass traffic on uncompressed, and the 200 OK comes back compressed because the Via header asked for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A SIP entity receiving a compressed message has to decompress it and to parse it. This requires slightly more processing power than only parsing a message, so a denial of service attack using compressed messages would be slightly worse than an attack with uncompressed messages.

An attacker inserting the parameter comp=sigcomp in a SIP message could make a SIP entity send compressed messages to another SIP entity that did not support SigComp. Appropriate integrity mechanisms should be used to avoid this attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressed messages take a little more work to handle, which makes a flood attack slightly more effective. An attacker could also slip the parameter into a message to make one end send compressed messages to an end that cannot read them, so the messages need integrity protection.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT DNS ENTRIES ONE SERVER WOULD NEED

data.title: Compression parameters
data.code:
compression-param  =  "comp=" ("sigcomp" / other-compression)
other-compression  =  token

via-compression    =  "comp" EQUAL ("sigcomp" / other-compression)
other-compression  =  token

viz.caption: THE INVITE TRANSACTION THROUGH TWO PROXIES

messages.note: Compressed: P1 is configured for it.

messages.label: (2) INVITE
messages.note: P1 does not use compression by default.

messages.label: (3) INVITE
messages.note: P2 sends it uncompressed and Record-Routes itself.

messages.label: (5) 200 OK
messages.note: P2 adds comp=sigcomp to its Record-Route entry.

messages.note: Sent directly to P2, which did not Record-Route.
